source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 24 (PDF 118-133, printed 115-130); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 24 (Organic Nitrogen Compounds), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 Organic nitrogen compounds form the basis of life in the form of:
blocks.explanation: Organic nitrogen compounds form the basis of life as amino acids and nucleotides, which make proteins (24.1).

book_ref.quote: They form the basis of life in the form of amino acids and nucleotides

blocks.prompt: 2 Nylon, Kevlar® and polyurethane, found in every home and office, are:
blocks.explanation: The chapter names nylon, Kevlar® and polyurethane as nitrogen containing polymers (24.1).

book_ref.quote: Nylon, Kevlar®, and polyurethane are the nitrogen containing polymers

blocks.prompt: 3 Caffeine in coffee and theobromine in chocolate are both:
blocks.explanation: The Interesting Information box says caffeine and theobromine are both organic nitrogen compounds (24.1).

book_ref.quote: Caffeine in coffee and theobromine in chocolate both are organic nitrogen compounds

blocks.prompt: 4 Amines are considered as organic derivatives of:
blocks.explanation: In amines, alkyl or aryl groups replace one, two or three hydrogen atoms of ammonia (24.1).

book_ref.quote: Amines are considered as organic derivatives of ammonia

blocks.prompt: 5 Amines are classified as primary, secondary and tertiary on the basis of:

options.text: the number of carbon atoms in the longest chain
the number of hydrogen atoms of ammonia replaced by alkyl or aryl groups
the number of nitrogen atoms in the molecule
the type of carbon atom that carries the –NH₂ group

blocks.explanation: The number of H atoms of ammonia replaced by alkyl or aryl groups is the basis of the classification (24.1).

book_ref.quote: The number of hydrogen atoms replaced by alky or aryl groups provides a foundation

blocks.prompt: 6 In the IUPAC system, amines are named as:
blocks.explanation: In IUPAC nomenclature amines are referred to as alkanamines, e.g. methanamine, ethanamine (24.1).

book_ref.quote: In IUPAC nomenclature system, amines are referred to as alkanamines

blocks.prompt: 7 Which one of the following is a primary amine?
blocks.explanation: Propan-1-amine has one alkyl group on –NH₂, so it is primary; the others are secondary or tertiary (24.1).

book_ref.quote: Primary amines: methanamine, ethanamine, propan-1-amine and phenyl amine (aniline)

blocks.prompt: 8 Diphenyl amine is an example of a:
blocks.explanation: Two aryl groups are attached to the NH group in diphenyl amine, so it is a secondary amine (24.1).

book_ref.quote: Secondary amines: N-methylmethanamine, N-methylethanamine and diphenyl amine

blocks.prompt: 9 In a secondary amine such as N-methylmethanamine, the nitrogen atom carries:

options.text: two carbon groups and two hydrogen atoms
one carbon group and two hydrogen atoms
two carbon groups and one hydrogen atom (–NH–)
three carbon groups and no hydrogen atom

blocks.explanation: In secondary amines two alkyl or aryl groups are attached to an NH group, so N has only one H: CH₃–NH–CH₃ (24.1, book correction).

book_ref.quote: In secondary amines, two alky or aryl groups are attached to NH group

blocks.prompt: 10 The formula of N,N-dimethylmethanamine is:
blocks.explanation: N,N-dimethylmethanamine (trimethylamine) has three methyl groups on one nitrogen: (CH₃)₃N, a tertiary amine (24.1).

book_ref.quote: Tertiary amines: N,N-dimethylmethanamine and triphenylamine

blocks.prompt: 11 Triphenylamine is classified as a tertiary amine because:

options.text: three aryl groups are attached to the same nitrogen atom
its nitrogen is attached to a tertiary carbon atom

blocks.explanation: In tertiary amines three alkyl or aryl groups are attached to the same nitrogen atom (24.1).

book_ref.quote: In tertiary amines, three alkyl or aryl groups are attached to the same nitrogen atom

blocks.prompt: 12 Tetramethylammonium chloride, (CH₃)₄N⁺Cl⁻, is a:
blocks.explanation: Tetra-substituted nitrogen derivatives are termed quaternary ammonium salts (24.1).

book_ref.quote: Tetra-substituted nitrogen derivatives are also known, and are termed as quaternary ammonium salts

blocks.prompt: 13 Whether an amine is primary, secondary or tertiary is decided by the branching at:

options.text: the carbon atom attached to nitrogen
the last carbon atom of the chain
the carbon atom next to the benzene ring

blocks.explanation: For amines the branching at the nitrogen atom decides the class, unlike alcohols or alkyl halides (24.1).

book_ref.quote: the branching takes place at the nitrogen atom, rather than at the carbon atom attached to it

blocks.prompt: 14 The reaction of a halogenoalkane with ammonia to give a primary amine is a:
blocks.explanation: Primary amines are prepared by nucleophilic substitution reactions of halogenoalkanes with ammonia (24.2).

book_ref.quote: Primary amines can be prepared by the nucleophilic substitution reactions of halogenoalkanes with ammonia

blocks.prompt: 15 In preparing a primary amine from a halogenoalkane, excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure is used to:

options.text: avoid the formation of secondary amines or a mixture of products
convert the amine into an amide
remove the halogen as a gas

blocks.explanation: Excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure avoids the formation of secondary amines or a mixture of products (24.2).

book_ref.quote: Excess of ethanolic ammonia under pressure is used to avoid the formation of secondary amines

blocks.prompt: 16 When a halogenoalkane is in excess over ammonia, the major product is:
blocks.explanation: If NH₃ is in excess the major product is a primary amine; if the halogenoalkane is in excess, a tertiary amine (24.2).

book_ref.quote: if halogenoalkane is in excess, tertiary amine is the major product

blocks.prompt: 17 Bromoethane reacts with excess ethanolic ammonia under high pressure to give:
blocks.explanation: CH₃CH₂Br + NH₃ (excess) → CH₃CH₂NH₂ (ethanamine), a primary amine (24.2).

book_ref.quote: Bromoethane and excess ammonia give ethanamine

blocks.prompt: 18 Reduction of propanenitrile with H₂/Ni or LiAlH₄ gives:
blocks.explanation: Primary amines are prepared by reducing alkanenitriles: CH₃CH₂CN → CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ (propan-1-amine) (24.2).

book_ref.quote: propanenitrile is reduced with H₂/Ni or LiAlH₄ ro prepare propane-1-amine

blocks.prompt: 19 Nitroethane is reduced with LiAlH₄ to form:
blocks.explanation: Nitroalkanes are reduced by LiAlH₄ to primary amines; nitroethane gives ethanamine (24.2).

book_ref.quote: Nitroalkanes are reduced in the presence of LiAlH₄ resulting in the formation of primary amines

blocks.prompt: 20 Reduction of alkanamides by LiAlH₄ gives primary amines in good yield because:

options.text: the reaction is carried out in water
the amide loses one carbon atom
no byproduct is formed in this reaction

blocks.explanation: Alkanamides are reduced by LiAlH₄ to primary amines in good yield since no byproduct is formed (24.2).

book_ref.quote: Alkanamides are reduced by LiAlH₄ to form primary amines in good yield

blocks.prompt: 21 The Hofmann reaction of propanamide (CH₃CH₂CONH₂) gives:
blocks.explanation: The Hofmann reaction yields an amine with one carbon less than the amide: a 3-carbon amide gives the 2-carbon ethanamine (24.2).

book_ref.quote: This reaction yields the amine with one carbon less than the starting amide.

blocks.prompt: 22 Methanamine reacts with bromoethane in ethanol under pressure to form:
blocks.explanation: Alkylation of a primary amine by a halogenoalkane gives a secondary amine: CH₃NH₂ + CH₃CH₂Br → CH₃NHCH₂CH₃ (24.2).

book_ref.quote: Secondary amines can be prepared by the alkylation of primary amines

blocks.prompt: 23 Secondary amines can be prepared by the reduction of:
blocks.explanation: Reduction of N-substituted amides gives secondary amines, e.g. N-methylethanamide → N-methylethanamine (24.2).

book_ref.quote: Secondary amines are also prepared by the reduction of N-substituted amides

blocks.prompt: 24 In the reduction CH₃CONHCH₃ → CH₃CH₂NHCH₃, the balanced equation uses:

options.text: H₂ only, and no water is formed

blocks.explanation: CH₃CONHCH₃ + 2H₂ → CH₃CH₂NHCH₃ + H₂O; the C=O oxygen leaves as water (24.2, book correction).

book_ref.quote: Reduction of N-methylethanamide to N-methylethanamine

blocks.prompt: 25 Phenylamine can be prepared from chlorobenzene by:
blocks.explanation: Ammonolysis of chlorobenzene (reaction with ammonia) gives phenylamine (24.2).

book_ref.quote: Ammonolysis is a reaction in which an ammonia molecule is broken down

blocks.prompt: 26 Reduction of nitrobenzene gives:
blocks.explanation: Phenylamine can also be prepared by the reduction of nitrobenzene (24.2).

book_ref.quote: Phenyl amine can also be prepared by the reduction of nitrobenzene

blocks.prompt: 27 Which amide gives phenylamine in the Hofmann reaction?
blocks.explanation: Phenylamine is prepared by the Hofmann reaction of benzamide, C₆H₅CONH₂ (one carbon is lost) (24.2).

book_ref.quote: Hofmann reaction of benzamide

blocks.prompt: 28 Water-soluble amines form weakly alkaline solutions because they:

options.text: react partially with water forming OH⁻ ions
react completely with water forming H₃O⁺

blocks.explanation: Like ammonia, they react partially with water: RNH₂ + H₂O ⇌ RNH₃⁺ + OH⁻ (24.3.1).

book_ref.quote: The amines which are soluble in water form weakly alkine solutions

blocks.prompt: 29 The basicity of amines depends on:

options.text: the availability of the lone pair of electrons on nitrogen
the number of carbon atoms in the molecule
the solubility of the amine in ether

blocks.explanation: Basicity depends on how available the nitrogen lone pair is for a proton (24.3.1).

book_ref.quote: The basicity of amines depends on the availability of the “lone pair” of electrons on the nitrogen atom

blocks.prompt: 30 A stronger base has:

options.text: a smaller Kb and a larger pKb
a larger Kb and a larger pKb
a larger Kb and a smaller pKb
a smaller Kb and a smaller pKb

blocks.explanation: The larger the Kb (or smaller the pKb), the stronger the base (24.3.1).

book_ref.quote: The Larger the Kb (or smaller the pKb), the stronger is the base

blocks.prompt: 31 Alkyl groups attached to the nitrogen atom of an amine:
blocks.explanation: Electron-donating alkyl groups increase basicity; electron-withdrawing groups decrease it (24.3.1).

book_ref.quote: electron-donating alkyl groups attached to the nitrogen atom increase the basicity of amines

blocks.prompt: 32 According to the chapter, a stronger base is mostly also a stronger:
blocks.explanation: Basicity is mostly an indicator of the stronger nucleophilic character of a compound (24.3.1).

book_ref.quote: Basicity is also an indicator of the stronger nucleophilic character of a compound, mostly

blocks.prompt: 33 From Table 24.1, the correct order of basic strength is:
blocks.explanation: pKb values: ethanamine 3.29 < ammonia 4.75 < phenylamine 9.38; the smallest pKb is the strongest base (24.3.1).

book_ref.quote: Table 24.1 The basicity of some amines

blocks.prompt: 34 The pKb of ethanamine given in Table 24.1 is:
blocks.explanation: Ethanamine has Kb = 5.1 × 10⁻⁴ and pKb = 3.29; 4.75 belongs to ammonia (24.3.1, book correction).

book_ref.quote: Its own Table 24.1 gives ethanamine pKb = 3.29

blocks.prompt: 35 The Kb of phenylamine (aniline) in Table 24.1 is:
blocks.explanation: Phenylamine has Kb = 4.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ (pKb = 9.38), the weakest base in the table (24.3.1).

book_ref.quote: Table 24.1 The basicity of some amines

blocks.prompt: 36 Using Kb values from Table 24.1 (ethanamine 5.1 × 10⁻⁴, ammonia 1.8 × 10⁻⁵), ethanamine is a stronger base than ammonia by a factor of about:

book_ref.quote: Its own Table 24.1 gives ethanamine pKb = 3.29 (Kb = 5.1 × 10⁻⁴)

blocks.prompt: 37 An amine has Kb = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴. Taking pKb = –log Kb, its pKb is:
blocks.explanation: pKb = –log(1.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 4.00; it is slightly stronger than ammonia (pKb 4.75) (24.3.1).

book_ref.quote: The Larger the Kb (or smaller the pKb), the stronger is the base

blocks.prompt: 38 Phenylamine is a weaker base than ammonia because:

options.text: the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised over the benzene ring
phenylamine has no lone pair on nitrogen
the benzene ring donates electrons to nitrogen
phenylamine is completely insoluble in acids

blocks.explanation: In phenylamine the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised over the benzene ring, so it is less available for a proton (24.3.1).

book_ref.quote: in phenylamine, the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom is delocalized over the benzene ring

blocks.prompt: 39 In phenylamine (Figure 24.1), the lone pair of the planar nitrogen atom is in:

options.text: an sp³ orbital pointing away from the ring
a p orbital that overlaps the delocalised π electrons of the ring

blocks.explanation: The nitrogen is planar with its lone pair in a p orbital, which overlaps the ring's delocalised π electrons (24.3.1).

book_ref.quote: The nitrogen atom is planar, with its lone pair in a p orbital

blocks.prompt: 40 When ethanamine reacts with hydrogen chloride, the bond formed between nitrogen and the proton is a:
blocks.explanation: Nitrogen donates its electron pair to a proton, forming a dative bond and the salt CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺Cl⁻ (24.3.1).

book_ref.quote: the nitrogen atom donates an electron pair to form a dative bond with a proton

blocks.prompt: 41 Lemon juice sprinkled on fish makes it less smelly because:

options.text: citric acid oxidises the fish protein
citric acid reacts with the basic amine (trimethylamine)
lemon juice dissolves the fish oil
the amine reacts with water in the juice to form an amide

blocks.explanation: The smell is from trimethylamine; citric acid in lemon juice reacts with this base to form a less smelly salt (24.3.1).

book_ref.quote: The foul smell from fish is due to N,N-dimethylmethanamine (trimethylamine)

blocks.text: 24.3.2 Distinction between Primary and Secondary Amines

blocks.prompt: 42 Primary, secondary and tertiary aliphatic amines are distinguished by their reaction with:
blocks.explanation: Aliphatic amines are identified by reacting them with nitric(III) acid, HNO₂ (24.3.2).

book_ref.quote: are identified and distinguished by reacting them with nitric (III) acid (nitrous acid)

blocks.prompt: 43 The formation of diazonium salts from primary amines and nitrous acid is called:
blocks.explanation: Primary amines react with nitrous acid to form diazonium salts; the process is called diazotization (24.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Primary amines react with nitrous acid to form diazonium salts

blocks.prompt: 44 On adding nitrous acid, which amine shows bubbles of nitrogen gas?
blocks.explanation: Only primary amines give N₂ bubbles with nitrous acid; propan-1-amine is primary (24.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Primary amines react with nitrous acid to produce nitrogen gas (seen as bubbles)

blocks.prompt: 45 A secondary amine reacts with nitrous acid to form:

options.text: an N-nitrosoamine, a yellow oily liquid
a diazonium salt with nitrogen bubbles
a soluble nitrite salt with no visible change

blocks.explanation: Secondary amines form N-nitrosoamines, seen as a yellow oily liquid (24.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Secondary amines form N-nitrosoamines (yellow oily liquid) on reaction with nitrous acid

blocks.prompt: 46 When nitrous acid is added to a tertiary amine:

options.text: a soluble nitrite salt forms with no visible sign of reaction

blocks.explanation: Tertiary amines form soluble nitrite salts; there is no visible sign of reaction (24.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Tertiary amines react with nitrous acid to form soluble nitrite salts

blocks.prompt: 47 Ethanamine reacts with nitrous acid (with HCl) to give, first of all:
blocks.explanation: Ethanamine, a primary amine, is diazotized to ethane diazonium chloride, which gives off N₂ (24.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Ethanamine and nitrous acid give ethane diazonium chloride

blocks.prompt: 48 An unknown amine gives a yellow oily liquid with nitrous acid. It could be:
blocks.explanation: A yellow oily N-nitrosoamine shows a secondary amine, e.g. N-methylethanamine (24.3.2).

book_ref.quote: N-methylethanamine and nitrous acid give an N-nitrosoamine

blocks.prompt: 49 The two types of reactions of phenylamine are due to:

options.text: the benzene ring and the C=O group
the benzene ring and the –NH₂ group
the –CN group and the benzene ring

blocks.explanation: Phenylamine reacts due to the benzene ring and due to the –NH₂ group (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: Phenylamine gives two types of reactions:

blocks.prompt: 50 Since the nitrogen of phenylamine is planar with its lone pair in a p orbital, its hybridisation is taken as:
blocks.explanation: A planar nitrogen with its lone pair in a p orbital is sp² hybridised, like the ring carbons (24.3.3, book correction).

book_ref.quote: Hybridisation in phenylamine: sp2 ring carbons and the nitrogen atom

blocks.prompt: 51 In electrophilic substitution of phenylamine, the –NH₂ group directs the incoming electrophile to:
blocks.explanation: The amino group is ortho-para directing, so the electrophile attacks at o and p positions (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: The amino group (–NH₂) is an ortho-para directing group

blocks.prompt: 52 Phenylamine reacts with bromine water to give:
blocks.explanation: Both ortho positions and the para position are brominated in a single reaction, giving 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: Bromination of phenylamine to 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine

blocks.prompt: 53 Bromination of phenylamine is faster than that of benzene because the –NH₂ group:

options.text: removes the π electrons of the ring
makes the benzene ring fairly reactive

blocks.explanation: The amino group makes the benzene ring fairly reactive, especially at o and p positions (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: Hence, bromination of phenylamine is faster than benzene

blocks.prompt: 54 The functional group of diazo compounds is:
blocks.explanation: Compounds with the diazonium ion –N⁺≡N (diazo group) as functional group are diazo compounds (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: The organic compounds having diazonium ion, –N⁺≡N (diazo group) as a functional group are called diazo compounds

blocks.prompt: 55 For diazotization, nitrous acid is prepared in situ from:
blocks.explanation: Nitrous acid is unstable and is prepared in situ from sodium nitrite and HCl (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: Nitrous acid is unstable and is prepared in situ by the reaction of sodium nitrite and HCl

blocks.prompt: 56 During diazotization of phenylamine the mixture is kept below 10 °C because:

options.text: diazonium salts are unstable and decompose giving off N₂

blocks.explanation: Diazonium salts are unstable and decompose easily, giving off N₂, even at room temperature (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: The reaction mixture is kept below 10 °C using ice

blocks.prompt: 57 When phenyldiazonium chloride is hydrolysed (warmed with water), the organic product is:
blocks.explanation: Hydrolysis of phenyldiazonium chloride gives phenol (with loss of N₂) (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: Diazotisation of phenylamine and hydrolysis of phenyldiazonium chloride to phenol

blocks.prompt: 58 Which statement about diazonium salts is correct?

options.text: Alkyl diazonium salts are more stable than aryl diazonium salts
Both alkyl and aryl diazonium salts are stable at room temperature
Alkyl diazonium salts cannot be isolated, but aryl diazonium salts are fairly stable at low temperature
Aryl diazonium salts cannot be prepared at all

blocks.explanation: Alkyl diazonium salts are highly unstable under all conditions; aryl diazonium salts are fairly stable at low temperatures (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: The alkyl diazonium salts are highly unstable under all conditions and therefore cannot be isolated

blocks.prompt: 59 The extra stability of aromatic diazonium salts is due to:

options.text: delocalisation of the positive charge over the aromatic ring
the absence of nitrogen in the ring

blocks.explanation: Aryl diazonium ions are more stable because the positive charge is delocalised over the aromatic ring (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: is due to the delocalization of the positive charge over the aromatic ring

blocks.prompt: 60 Benzene diazonium salts are important in organic synthesis as:
blocks.explanation: Benzene diazonium salts are important intermediates in the synthesis of many organic compounds (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: Benzene diazonium salts are the important intermediates in the synthesis of many organic compounds

blocks.prompt: 61 Reactions of aryl diazonium salts with strongly activated aromatic compounds such as phenols and amines are called:
blocks.explanation: These are coupling reactions; their products contain the –N=N– bond (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: are called coupling reactions

blocks.prompt: 62 In a coupling reaction the diazonium ion acts as:
blocks.explanation: The positively charged diazonium ion acts as an electrophile and substitutes into the ring of phenol (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: In the coupling reaction, the positively charged diazonium ion acts as an electrophile

blocks.prompt: 63 The diazonium ion substitutes into the benzene ring of phenol at the:
blocks.explanation: It substitutes into the benzene ring of phenol at the para position (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: It substitutes into the benzene ring of phenol at the para position

blocks.prompt: 64 Coupling of a diazonium salt with phenol is carried out in:
blocks.explanation: Coupling with phenol occurs in mild alkaline solution; with aromatic amines in mild acidic conditions (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: Coupling with phenol occurs in mild alkaline solution and with aromatic amines in mild acidic conditions

blocks.prompt: 65 Coupling of a diazonium salt with an aromatic amine takes place in:
blocks.explanation: With aromatic amines coupling occurs in mild acidic conditions (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: Coupling with phenol occurs in mild alkaline solution and with aromatic amines in mild acidic conditions

blocks.prompt: 66 In the last step of the mechanism of coupling with phenol, the intermediate:
blocks.explanation: The ring intermediate loses a proton, –H⁺, restoring the benzene ring (24.3.3, book correction).

book_ref.quote: The last step of the printed mechanism shows ‘–H’; a proton is lost, –H⁺, as drawn above.

blocks.prompt: 67 p-Dimethylaminoazobenzene (butter yellow) is no longer used in food because it is:
blocks.explanation: Butter yellow was once used in food, but its use is forbidden because it is carcinogenic (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: p-Dimethylaminoazo benzene is called Butter yellow

blocks.prompt: 68 Methyl orange, an acid-base indicator, is prepared by coupling diazotized sulfanilic acid with:
blocks.explanation: Methyl orange is prepared from diazotized sulfanilic acid and N,N-dimethylphenylamine (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: Methyl orange is an acid-base indicator and is prepared from diazotized sulfanilic acid

blocks.prompt: 69 The group responsible for the intense colour of azo dyes (the chromophore) is:
blocks.explanation: The azo group (Ph–N=N–Ph) is the chromophore responsible for the intense colour (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: This group is responsible for the intense colour of the dyes

blocks.prompt: 70 The colour of an azo dye depends upon:

options.text: what other groups are attached to the benzene rings
the temperature at which it is stored
the number of nitrogen atoms in the azo group
whether it is a solid or a liquid

blocks.explanation: Colours range from yellow and orange to red, blue and green depending on the other groups on the rings (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: ranging from yellow and orange to red, blue and green depending upon what other groups

blocks.prompt: 71 Azo dyes are often present in:
blocks.explanation: The chapter notes that different food colours often contain azo dyes (24.3.3).

book_ref.quote: Different food colours often contain azo dyes.

blocks.prompt: 72 Alkanenitriles contain the functional group:
blocks.explanation: Organic compounds containing the –CN functional group are alkanenitriles (24.4).

book_ref.quote: The organic compounds containing -CN functional group are called alkanenitriles

blocks.prompt: 73 The most important application of alkanenitriles mentioned in the chapter is their:
blocks.explanation: Their most important application is hydrolysis to carboxylic acids, with dilute acid or dilute alkali (24.4).

book_ref.quote: the most important applications of alkanenitriles is their hydrolysis

blocks.prompt: 74 In the acid hydrolysis CH₃CN + 2H₂O + HCl →, the inorganic product is:
blocks.explanation: CH₃CN + 2H₂O + HCl → CH₃COOH + NH₄Cl; the nitrogen ends up as ammonium chloride (24.4).

book_ref.quote: When a nitrile is heated with a dilute acid

blocks.prompt: 75 Propanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CN, is heated with dilute hydrochloric acid. The carboxylic acid formed is:
blocks.explanation: Acid hydrolysis turns –CN into –COOH with the same carbon count: CH₃CH₂CN → CH₃CH₂COOH (24.4).

book_ref.quote: such as dilute hydrochloric acid or dilute sulphuric acid, a carboxylic acid is formed

blocks.prompt: 76 Heating ethanenitrile with dilute NaOH solution gives:
blocks.explanation: CH₃CN + H₂O + NaOH → CH₃COONa + NH₃(g) (24.4).

book_ref.quote: When a nitrile is heated with a dilute sodium hydroxide solution

blocks.prompt: 77 After alkaline hydrolysis of a nitrile, the free carboxylic acid is obtained by:
blocks.explanation: The sodium salt is acidified: CH₃COONa + HCl → CH₃COOH + NaCl (24.4).

book_ref.quote: which on acidification with dilute hydrochloric acid gives free carboxylic acid

blocks.prompt: 78 The functional group of an amide is:
blocks.explanation: Amides contain the –CO–NH₂ functional group (24.5).

book_ref.quote: Amides contain the functional group –CO–NH₂

blocks.prompt: 79 Amides are sometimes called acid amides because they:
blocks.explanation: Since amides are prepared from carboxylic acids they are still sometimes called acid amides (24.5).

book_ref.quote: that is why amides are still sometimes called as “acid amides”

blocks.prompt: 80 Ethanoyl chloride reacts with ammonia at room temperature to give:
blocks.explanation: Acyl chlorides react with ammonia to form amides: CH₃COCl + NH₃ → CH₃CONH₂ + HCl (24.5).

book_ref.quote: By the reaction of acyl chlorides with ammonia

blocks.prompt: 81 The reaction of an acyl chloride with a primary amine gives:
blocks.explanation: Acyl chlorides react with primary amines to form N-substituted amides (24.5).

book_ref.quote: By the reaction of acyl chlorides with primary amines

blocks.prompt: 82 When acyl chlorides react with ammonia or primary amines, the white fumes released are of:
blocks.explanation: The reactions take place at room temperature, releasing white fumes of HCl (24.5).

book_ref.quote: releasing white fumes of hydrogen chloride (HCl)

blocks.prompt: 83 An excess of ammonia or amine is used when making amides from acyl chlorides because:

options.text: ammonia acts as a catalyst only
the HCl formed reacts with another molecule of ammonia or amine to form a salt
the amide reacts with excess acyl chloride
excess ammonia lowers the boiling point

blocks.explanation: The HCl produced reacts with another molecule of ammonia or amine to form a salt, so excess is used to complete the reaction (24.5).

book_ref.quote: Therefore, an excess of ammonia or amine is used to ensure complete reaction.

blocks.prompt: 84 Which amide is a liquid at room temperature?
blocks.explanation: All amides except methanamide, which is a liquid, are solids with sharp melting points (24.5).

book_ref.quote: All amides except methanamide, which is a liquid, are solid with sharp melting point

blocks.prompt: 85 The quite high boiling points of amides are due to:

options.text: their very high molar masses only

blocks.explanation: Amides have high boiling points as a consequence of strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding (24.5).

book_ref.quote: which is a consequence of strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding

blocks.prompt: 86 As the number of alkyl substituents on the nitrogen of an amide increases, its melting and boiling points:

options.text: decrease, as sites for hydrogen bonding diminish
increase, as the amide becomes ionic

blocks.explanation: In N-substituted amides the melting and boiling points decrease as the sites for hydrogen bonding diminish (24.5).

book_ref.quote: the melting and boiling points decrease as the sites for hydrogen bonding diminish

blocks.prompt: 87 In water, amides form:
blocks.explanation: Amides are less basic than aliphatic amines; unlike amines they form neutral solutions in water (24.5).

book_ref.quote: Unlike amines, amides form neutral solutions in water

blocks.prompt: 88 Amides are less basic than aliphatic amines because:

options.text: amides have no lone pair on nitrogen
the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised with the oxygen of the carbonyl group
alkyl groups withdraw electrons from nitrogen

blocks.explanation: Resonance delocalises the nitrogen lone pair towards the carbonyl oxygen, reducing its availability (24.5).

book_ref.quote: the lone pair on nitrogen participates in delocalization with oxygen of carbonyl group

blocks.prompt: 89 Compared with the C–N bond in an amine, the C–N bond in an amide is:

options.text: longer, because of partial double bond character
shorter, because of partial double bond character
longer, because nitrogen is more basic

blocks.explanation: Resonance gives the amide C–N bond some double bond character, so it is shorter than a usual C–N single bond (24.5).

book_ref.quote: C-N bond lengths in an amide and in an amine

blocks.prompt: 90 Among all acid derivatives, amides are:
blocks.explanation: Amides are the least reactive acid derivatives because nitrogen's lone pair reduces the +δ charge on the carbonyl carbon (24.5).

book_ref.quote: Amides are the least reactive of all acid derivatives

blocks.prompt: 91 Reactions of amides generally require:

options.text: prolonged heating or catalysts (acid or base)

blocks.explanation: Amide reactions are slow and need prolonged heating or acid/base catalysts (24.5).

book_ref.quote: Reactions of amides are generally slow and require prolonged heating or catalysts

blocks.prompt: 92 Acid hydrolysis of ethanamide gives ethanoic acid and:
blocks.explanation: Unsubstituted amides on acid hydrolysis yield the carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt (24.5).

book_ref.quote: Unsubstituted amides yield carboxylic acids ammonium salt

blocks.prompt: 93 Base hydrolysis of ethanamide with NaOH gives:
blocks.explanation: In base hydrolysis the products are the salt of the carboxylic acid and ammonia (24.5).

book_ref.quote: In the base-catalyzed reaction, the products are the salts of carboxylic acids and ammonia

blocks.prompt: 94 Amides are reduced to primary amines by:
blocks.explanation: Amides are reduced to primary amines with lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III), LiAlH₄, in dry ether (24.5).

book_ref.quote: Amides are reduced to primary amines with lithium tetrahydridoaluminate (III) in dry ethoxyethane (ether)

blocks.prompt: 95 Benzamide, C₆H₅CONH₂, is reduced by LiAlH₄. The product is:
blocks.explanation: LiAlH₄ reduces only the C=O to CH₂; the benzene ring stays: C₆H₅CONH₂ → C₆H₅CH₂NH₂ (24.5, book correction).

book_ref.quote: Reduction of ethanamide and benzamide with LiAlH4

blocks.prompt: 96 Amino acids contain:

options.text: a basic –NH₂ group and an acidic –COOH group

blocks.explanation: Amino acids contain the basic amino group (–NH₂) and the acidic carboxylic acid group (–COOH) (24.6).

book_ref.quote: Amino acids are an important group of compounds that contain:

blocks.prompt: 97 α-Amino acids are also called:
blocks.explanation: The general amino acid is a 2-aminocarboxylic acid, also called an α-amino acid (24.6).

book_ref.quote: The general structure of amino acids (2-aminocarboxylic acid), also called α-amino acids

blocks.prompt: 98 In the formation of a zwitter ion, the proton moves:

options.text: from the amino group to the carboxyl group
from the R group to the carboxyl group
from water to the R group
from the carboxyl group to the amino group

blocks.explanation: The proton goes from –COOH to –NH₂, giving H₃N⁺–CH(R)–COO⁻ (24.6).

book_ref.quote: In the formation of a Zwitter ion, the proton goes from the carboxyl group to the amino group

blocks.prompt: 99 The dipolar structure (zwitter ion) of an amino acid is also called:
blocks.explanation: The dipolar structure, with + and – ends in one molecule, is also called the internal salt (24.6).

book_ref.quote: The dipolar structure is also called the internal salt

blocks.prompt: 100 The correct zwitter ion of glycine is:
blocks.explanation: In the zwitter ion the groups carry charges: –NH₃⁺ and –COO⁻; for glycine R = H (24.6, book correction).

book_ref.quote: The printed zwitterion shows ‘COO’ and ‘Nh₃’ without charges

blocks.prompt: 101 In the simplest amino acid, glycine, the R group is:
blocks.explanation: Glycine (aminoethanoic acid) is the simplest amino acid; its R is a hydrogen atom (24.6).

book_ref.quote: The simplest amino acid is glycine (aminoethanoic acid) in which R is a hydrogen atom

blocks.prompt: 102 The IUPAC-type name of alanine is:
blocks.explanation: Alanine is 2-aminopropanoic acid, with R = –CH₃ (24.6).

book_ref.quote: Alanine (2-amino propanoic acid) is an amino acid in which the R group is the methyl group

blocks.prompt: 103 Which α-amino acid is not chiral?
blocks.explanation: Except glycine (R = H, two H atoms on the α-carbon), all α-amino acids are chiral (24.6).

book_ref.quote: Except glycine all α-amino acids are chiral.

blocks.prompt: 104 Essential amino acids are those which:
blocks.explanation: Essential amino acids are those the body cannot synthesise, so they must come from food (24.6).

book_ref.quote: essential (body cannot synthesis)

blocks.text: 24.6.1 Acidic and Basic Properties of Amino Acids

blocks.prompt: 105 Amino acids are described as amphoteric because they:

options.text: show both acidic and basic properties

blocks.explanation: Amino acids are amphoteric, showing both acidic and basic properties (24.6.1).

book_ref.quote: Amino acids are amphoteric, i.e., they show both acidic and basic properties

blocks.prompt: 106 Compared with carboxylic acids and amines, amino acids are:

options.text: more acidic than carboxylic acids and more basic than amines
less acidic than most carboxylic acids and less basic than most amines
more acidic than carboxylic acids but less basic than amines

blocks.explanation: Amino acids are less acidic than most carboxylic acids and less basic than most amines (24.6.1).

book_ref.quote: they are less acidic than most carboxylic acids, and are less basic than most amines

blocks.prompt: 107 In a zwitter ion, the acidic part and the basic part respectively are:
blocks.explanation: The acidic part is –NH₃⁺ (it gives a proton) and the basic part is –COO⁻ (it accepts a proton) (24.6.1).

book_ref.quote: In fact, the acidic part of the amino acid molecule is –NH₃⁺, group, not –COO⁻ group

blocks.prompt: 108 For the zwitter ion H₃N⁺–CH(R)–COO⁻, the approximate pKa (loss of H⁺ from –NH₃⁺) is:
blocks.explanation: H₃N⁺–CH(R)–COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ H₂N–CH(R)–COO⁻ + H₃O⁺, pKa ≈ 10; RNH₃⁺ is a weaker acid than RCOOH (24.6.1).

book_ref.quote: RNH₃⁺ is a weaker acid than RCOOH, as shown below:

blocks.prompt: 109 In aqueous solution, an amino acid exists in equilibrium between:

options.text: a cationic form, the dipolar ion and an anionic form
a diazonium salt and an azo compound
a nitrile and a carboxylic acid

blocks.explanation: An equilibrium exists between the dipolar ion and cationic and anionic forms of the amino acid (24.6.1).

book_ref.quote: In the aqueous solution, an equilibrium exists between the dipolar ion and a cationic and an anionic form

blocks.prompt: 110 The pH at which the concentration of the zwitter ion of an amino acid is maximum is called its:
blocks.explanation: This pH is the isoelectric point (pI); each amino acid has its own unique pI (24.6.1).

book_ref.quote: This pH is called the isoelectric point (pI)

blocks.text: 24.6.2 Separation of Amino Acids by Electrophoresis

blocks.prompt: 111 Electrophoresis separates amino acids on the basis of their:
blocks.explanation: Electrophoresis separates amino acids in a mixture based on their charge (different pI values) (24.6.2).

book_ref.quote: is used to separate amino acid in a mixture based on their charge

blocks.prompt: 112 In electrophoresis, the mixture is applied to filter paper or gel placed in:

options.text: a buffered solution between two electrodes
a column packed with silica only

blocks.explanation: A few drops are applied to a filter paper or gel placed in a buffered solution between two electrodes (24.6.2).

book_ref.quote: a few drops of the mixture are applied to a filter paper or gel that is placed in a buffered solution between two electrodes

blocks.prompt: 113 In electrophoresis at pH 6.0, an amino acid with pI = 9.7 moves towards the:

options.text: neither electrode; it stays at the start
edge of the paper away from both electrodes

blocks.explanation: pI (9.7) > pH (6.0), so the amino acid bears a positive charge and migrates towards the cathode (24.6.2).

book_ref.quote: will migrate toward the cathode

blocks.prompt: 114 An amino acid with pI = 3.0 placed in a buffer of pH 6.0 will:

options.text: bear a negative charge and move to the anode
bear a positive charge and move to the cathode
carry no charge and stay at the start
bear a negative charge and move to the cathode

blocks.explanation: pI lower than pH: the amino acid is mainly negatively charged and migrates towards the anode (24.6.2).

book_ref.quote: An amino acid with a pI that is lower than the pH of the solution exists predominantly in a form that bears a negative charge

blocks.prompt: 115 At pH 6.0, two amino acids have pI values 7.6 and 10.8. Which moves faster, and towards which electrode?

options.text: the one with pI 7.6, towards the cathode
the one with pI 10.8, towards the cathode
the one with pI 10.8, towards the anode
both move at the same speed to the anode

blocks.explanation: Both have pI > pH (positive, to cathode); the greater difference (10.8 – 6.0 = 4.8 vs 1.6) migrates faster (24.6.2).

book_ref.quote: If the pI of an amino acid is greater than the pH of the solution

blocks.prompt: 116 Glycine and leucine have very similar pI values. In electrophoresis:

options.text: the lighter one moves more slowly
both stay at the starting line
the one with the larger molecular weight moves more slowly
they always move to opposite electrodes

blocks.explanation: With similar pI, the amino acid of larger molecular weight moves more slowly because the charge carries a greater mass (24.6.2).

book_ref.quote: the amino acid with the larger molecular weight will move more slowly

blocks.prompt: 117 In electrophoresis, the colourless amino acid spots are located with ninhydrin, which gives a:
blocks.explanation: Ninhydrin is the locating agent; it reacts with amino acids to give a purple product (24.6.2).

book_ref.quote: Ninhydrin is used as a locating agent, which reacts with amino acids to produce a purple product

blocks.prompt: 118 To actually separate an entire (large) mixture of amino acids, the chapter names:
blocks.explanation: Electrophoresis is only an analytical method; column chromatography is used to actually separate a mixture (24.6.2).

book_ref.quote: Electrophoresis cannot be used to separate large quantities of amino acids

blocks.prompt: 119 The molecule formed when two amino acids react together is a:
blocks.explanation: When two amino acids react together, the resulting molecule is a dipeptide (24.6.3).

book_ref.quote: When two amino acids react together, the resulting molecule is called a dipeptide

blocks.prompt: 120 A peptide bond is a type of:
blocks.explanation: An amide bond (–CO–NH–) between two amino acids is called a peptide bond or peptide link (24.6.3).

book_ref.quote: An amide bond between two amino acid molecules is also called a peptide bond or peptide link

blocks.prompt: 121 Formation of a dipeptide is a condensation reaction because:

options.text: a small molecule, water, is eliminated

blocks.explanation: It is a condensation reaction: a small molecule, water, is eliminated as the molecules join (24.6.3).

book_ref.quote: The reaction is a condensation reaction

blocks.prompt: 122 In forming a peptide link, the –COOH group of one amino acid reacts with:

options.text: the –COOH group of another amino acid
the –NH₂ group of another amino acid
the R group of the same amino acid

blocks.explanation: The acidic –COOH group of one amino acid reacts with the basic –NH₂ group of another (24.6.3).

book_ref.quote: The acidic -COOH group in one amino acid molecule reacts with the basic-NH₂ group

blocks.prompt: 123 A tetrapeptide is formed by the condensation of four amino acids. The number of water molecules eliminated is:
blocks.explanation: Each peptide link eliminates one water; four amino acids in a chain are joined by 3 links, so 3 H₂O (24.6.3).

book_ref.quote: a compound formed from the condensation reaction between three amino acids

blocks.prompt: 124 A compound formed by the condensation of a large number of amino acids is a:
blocks.explanation: A polypeptide is formed from the condensation between a large number of amino acids (24.6.3).

book_ref.quote: a compound formed from the condensation between a large number of amino acids

blocks.prompt: 125 At its isoelectric point, an amino acid in aqueous solution has:
blocks.explanation: The isoelectric point is the pH at which there is no overall charge on the amino acid (24.6.3 key words).

book_ref.quote: the pH value at which there is no overall charge on a particular amino acid

blocks.prompt: 126 The R group of lysine is:
blocks.explanation: Quick Check 24.5 gives lysine R = –CH₂–(CH₂)₃NH₂ and aspartic acid R = –CH₂–COOH (24.6.3).

book_ref.quote: The R groups in the amino acids aspartic acid and lysine are

blocks.prompt: 127 Aspartic acid has R = –CH₂–COOH. Compared with glycine, its R group adds an extra:
blocks.explanation: Aspartic acid's R group (–CH₂–COOH) carries a second, acidic –COOH group (24.6.3).

book_ref.quote: The R groups in the amino acids aspartic acid and lysine are
